column3: Pairs denial before full knowledge with the command to inspect the wrongdoers' outcome.
Offers repentance and transformed evil as a remedy, but not the focus's conscious denial.
Explicitly joins denial of signs, arrogant obedience, and a ruined people.
Gives Pharaoh's drowning as the inspected outcome of wrongdoers.
Opens the same passage by identifying the Quran's clear signs.
Sets certainty in the Lord of creation against the focus's inward certainty suppressed by denial.
Shares the command to inspect the retaliatory outcome of deniers.
Immediately frames wrongdoing, replacement with good, and mercy before the signs episode.
Shows certainty in divine signs producing steadfast, guiding action rather than denial.
Closely parallels Moses's signs to Pharaoh, their wrongdoing, and the corrupters' outcome.
Defines corrupters as those who damage the earth without repair.
Connects clear signs held within the learned to their denial by wrongdoers.
Repeats the command to inspect the eventual outcome of those warned.
Continues the same opening contrast by naming guidance and good news for believers.
The heavenly high horizon does not illuminate the blameworthy self-exaltation in the focus.
Shows deceivers lying against themselves as their false claims vanish, clarifying inward self-wronging.
Immediate predecessor: manifest signs are relabeled as obvious sorcery.
The elevated register is not a useful link to arrogant elevation here.
Combines obstructing God's path with the command to inspect corrupters' outcome.
Its replacement of evil with better conduct is only a secondary ethical counterpoint.
Challenges self-exaltation and contrasts it with God's just purification.
Calls for observing earlier peoples' end and states that they wronged themselves.
Same passage, but its believerly certainty and practice only provide a broad contrast.
Names the formed self without addressing certainty, denial, or its consequence.
Makes former wrongdoers' dwellings and their fate visible as a warning.
In the same surah, explicitly exposes the destructive outcome of plotting.
Divine exaltedness only contrasts indirectly with human arrogant elevation.
Addresses Pharaoh's late confession by recalling his prior rebellion and corruption.
Same opening passage: disbelief in the Hereafter leaves people confused in embellished deeds.
Directly prohibits elevation against Solomon, echoing the focus's condemned elevation.
Names a people as corrupters and seeks deliverance from them.
Same surah's testing of truthfulness offers only a distant contrast to denying known truth.
Links denial of divine signs to enduring recompense, though through a contrast route.
Portrays Pharaoh's elevation, oppression, and corruption in the earth.
Distinguishes belief from disbelief and leaves God knowing the corrupters.
Knowledge of certainty supplies a compact contrast to inward certainty denied in action.
Worldly advantages become punishment for disbelievers, but the link is general.
Same passage states the evil punishment and ultimate loss of disbelievers.
States the just rule that each self is repaid only for what it did.
Repeats the worldly-punishment motif without the focus's signs or conscious denial.
Same surah repeats the command to inspect the outcome of criminals.
Affirms certain truth, contrasting with certainty withheld from public affirmation.
Declares failure for whoever bears wrongdoing before the Living Sustainer.
Its teaching of dream interpretation does not materially develop this denial-and-outcome scene.
Shows leading criminals plotting while unknowingly plotting only against themselves.
Recalls earlier destroyed peoples while denying that God wrongs servants.
Same opening passage grounds the Quran in the Wise and Knowing source.
Matches certainty in the Lord of heavens and earth as a challenge to disbelief.
Explicitly opposes seeking elevation and corruption, assigning the outcome to the God-conscious.
Same surah describes royal invasion as corruption that humiliates a people.
Uses certainty for the arrival of death, not recognition and denial of signs.
Denies injustice or loss to faithful righteous actors, countering the focus's wrongdoing.
A directive on gentle speech does not add to the focus's scene.
Hidden reward for deeds has no substantial link beyond the word for self.
Names Pharaoh as exalted and among the transgressors.
Same passage begins Moses's call, but precedes the denial at issue.
Directly connects denial of God's signs with being turned away.
Explains that wrongdoers deny God's signs even when the messenger is not personally denied.
Same passage's call at the fire is contextual but not yet the response to signs.
Creation's signs for people of certainty offer a broad evidentiary contrast.
States that only disbelievers deny God's signs.
Pairs historical patterns with the command to inspect deniers' outcome.
Believers' rank through struggle does not develop the focus's moral failure.
Affirms that God does not will injustice for the worlds.
Same passage identifies the speaker to Moses but adds little to conscious denial.
Names Pharaoh's elevation and his persecution of those who believed Moses.
Makes the just accounting of every self explicit, including the smallest deed.
A demand for manifest authority in the hoopoe narrative only faintly echoes signs and proof.
Earthly signs for the certain provide a broad contrast to rejected signs.
Shows wrongful consumption returning as fire, an instance of consequence for injustice.
Prayer for protection from evil consequences is only a remedial parallel.
Addresses Pharaoh's side with a prohibition on exaltation and a manifest authority.
The self-directed consequence of hoarding is a distant instance of recompense.
Same passage supplies Moses's first sign before the later denial.
The tranquil self is a loose positive contrast to a self knowing yet denying.
Honored elevation of Idris does not clarify arrogant elevation.
Same surah's humiliation of resisters has only an indirect outcome link.
Pairing of selves does not develop inward certainty or denial.
Affirms certain truth, usefully contrasting the focus's suppressed certainty.
Connects each self's earning with just, swift recompense.
Calls revelation insight and guidance for the certain, but remains general.
An elevated garden is unrelated to the focus's blameworthy elevation.
Immediate context: Moses is sent with nine signs to Pharaoh and his defiantly immoral people.
God's knowledge of inward selves offers a limited contrast to hidden recognition.
Gives an explicit command to inspect the outcome of criminals.
Same surah's deliberation about strength and command does not materially add to the focus.
Self and wealth in the call to struggle are not relevant here.
Shows the destructive seizure and removal of wrongdoers.
Same surah's rejection of a gift is contextual but does not develop the focus's claim.
Challenges deniers whose failure to reach certainty follows reflection on creation.
Pairs clarification of signs with people being turned away from them.
Same surah later identifies people who lacked certainty in God's signs.
The difficult ascent is only a lexical coincidence with elevation.
Links disbelief to belated self-reproach under God's greater condemnation.
Permitted redress after suffering injustice does not illuminate conscious denial or corruption.
Connects concealed sinful speech and defiant conduct with the final evil destination.
Those seeking to mislead harm only themselves, with a distant self-wronging link.
The disclosure of what is hidden in the self is only a limited inward/outward parallel.
People knowingly choose harmful magic, illustrating knowledge joined to self-damaging disbelief.
Withholding charity harms the self and brings replacement, a general consequence pattern.
Those given the Book recognize the truth as they recognize their sons yet knowingly conceal it.
Challenges People of the Book for denying God's signs while themselves bearing witness.
Names knowingly concealing truth by mixing it with falsehood.
Those given the Book recognize the revelation, yet the self-losing still disbelieve.
States that Pharaoh's people denied the signs and were drowned for heedlessness.
Links wrongful self-exaltation to turning from signs and choosing the path of corruption.
Moses and Aaron bring signs to Pharaoh and his elite, who respond with arrogance and crime.
Returns to Moses's nine clear signs and Pharaoh's rejection of them.
Explicitly says Pharaoh was shown every sign but denied and refused.
Same surah makes the desolate homes of wrongdoers a visible outcome.
Directly confronts deniers of God's signs for rejecting what they had not encompassed.
Clear signs sent to Pharaoh are dismissed as magic and fabrication.
Pharaoh and his forces act arrogantly without right and wrongly deny their return to God.
Moses comes to Pharaoh with signs and clear authority in another direct retelling.
Disputing God's signs without authority is tied to a great pride in hearts.
Identifies pride as the motive of those disputing God's signs without authority.
Describes a people who arrogantly exalted themselves before receiving destructive punishment.
Moses is sent with signs to Pharaoh and his elite, who meet them with arrogance.
Depicts one who hears God's signs yet persists arrogantly as though he never heard them.
Pharaoh turns away from Moses's clear authority and labels him a magician or madman.
Pharaoh's claim to be the highest lord makes his self-exaltation explicit.
God's seizure of Pharaoh supplies a compressed statement of the consequence of that claim.
